where: Section 1: Four names that made the engine
problem: The four names are not in date order: Clerk (1878) is placed after Diesel (patent 1892, engine 1897). In a history section this reads as if Clerk came after Diesel, and a student revising by sequence will memorise the wrong order.
fix: List them as Lenoir 1860, Otto 1876, Clerk 1878, Diesel patent 1892 and working engine 1897, or say in one line that the entries are grouped by idea, not by date.

problem: "A two-stroke engine uses ports and scavenging" is stated as if it holds for every two-stroke. Large two-stroke diesel engines use an exhaust valve with uniflow scavenging and inlet ports only; piston-controlled ports alone are typical of small engines.
fix: Say: small two-stroke engines use piston-controlled inlet and exhaust ports with crankcase or pump scavenging; large two-stroke diesels use inlet ports with an exhaust valve.

problem: The chapter calls fuel one of the five classification labels, but the tree has branches only for ignition, stroke and cooling, with aspiration as a root note. Fuel appears nowhere, so the figure and the text do not match.
fix: Add a fuel branch (petrol, diesel, CNG/LPG, alcohol blend, hydrogen) to the tree, or add a line in the caption saying fuel is deliberately left out of this figure.

problem: "Petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG, alcohol blends and hydrogen are all used in production engines" puts hydrogen on the same footing as the others. Hydrogen IC engines have appeared only in small-series production; most hydrogen vehicles on the road are fuel-cell electric, not IC engines.
fix: Say that petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG and alcohol blends are in wide production use, while hydrogen has so far been used in only a few small-series IC engines and mostly in fuel cells.

problem: Cross-references such as "see four-stroke operation", "See SI and CI working principle", "See Chapter 1.3" and "See Unit 4, Cooling, Lubrication and Supercharging" are plain text, so a student reading on a phone cannot tap through to the chapter.
fix: Make each cross-reference a link to the target chapter, keeping the same wording.
